market_context: United States/general English; cooked chicken safety and food-thermometer use
title: Pink chicken: when it can be safely cooked and when it is not

seo.title: Pink chicken: can it still be safely cooked?
seo.meta_description: Pink color does not prove chicken is undercooked. The reliable test is 165 °F in the thickest part; myoglobin, bones, smoke and oven gases can leave pink tones.
seo.search_intent: Understand why cooked chicken can stay pink and how to verify doneness safely with a food thermometer.

excerpt: Chicken can remain pink even after reaching a safe internal temperature. USDA says color is not a reliable doneness test: poultry should reach at least 165 °F (73.9 °C) in the thickest appropriate area, measured away from bone.
content_html:
Pink chicken often gets treated as automatic proof of undercooking. USDA says color alone cannot tell you whether poultry is safe.

The reliable number is 165 °F

All poultry should reach a minimum internal temperature of 165 °F (73.9 °C). Measure in the thickest part of the meat and keep the thermometer tip away from bone.

For a whole bird, check the innermost thigh and wing and the thickest part of the breast. For a breast, thigh or drumstick, place the probe in the thickest section.

Safely cooked chicken can still be pink

USDA notes that properly cooked poultry can range from white to pink to tan. Hemoglobin and myoglobin pigments can retain color even after the meat has reached 165 °F.

Oven gases, grilling, smoking and small amounts of nitrates or nitrites can also produce or preserve pink tones.

Pink near the bone can be especially noticeable

In younger birds, bone marrow pigments can move through relatively porous bones and discolor nearby tissue. The effect may be more obvious in chicken that was frozen before cooking.

A pink patch next to a bone therefore does not prove the meat is unsafe if the surrounding meat reached the required temperature.

White meat can also be undercooked

The opposite mistake is equally important: chicken can turn white before it is hot enough to destroy harmful bacteria. Waiting for all visible pinkness to disappear is not a dependable safety method.

Clear juices are not a safety test either

The color of juices can vary for the same reasons as the meat. USDA emphasizes temperature, not clear juices, as the reliable measure of doneness.

How to measure a thin piece

For thin chicken breasts or cutlets, inserting an instant-read thermometer from the side helps position the sensing area in the center rather than close to the surface. Avoid touching bone, which can distort the reading.

Safe does not mean you must stop at exactly 165 °F

165 °F is the minimum USDA target for poultry. Breast meat cooked far beyond it can lose additional moisture and become dry, while thighs often develop a more tender texture at somewhat higher temperatures. Those are texture choices after the safety threshold is met.

Bottom line

Pink does not automatically mean raw, and white does not automatically mean safe. Use a food thermometer and verify at least 165 °F in the right place.

faq.question: Can fully cooked chicken still be pink?
faq.answer: Yes. USDA says safely cooked poultry can remain pink even after reaching 165 °F.

faq.question: Why is chicken pink near the bone?
faq.answer: Bone marrow and tissue pigments can discolor meat near the bone, especially in young or previously frozen birds.

faq.question: Are clear juices a reliable doneness test?
faq.answer: No. Internal temperature is much more reliable than meat color or juice color.
